Step 1 of 6

Welcome to Nugget

Nugget learns from your notes, mail and calendar, and helps you write, find and remember things. It runs on this computer, and you decide what it reads and what, if anything, leaves your computer.

Stays on this device
Everything Nugget indexes from your sources, and the knowledge it builds from them
Your chats and drafts when you use a local model
Your settings, encrypted with a key kept in your OS keychain
Leaves only when you choose
Requests to a cloud AI provider, if you set one up with your own key
Syncing with accounts you connect, such as Gmail or a CalDAV calendar
Model downloads, checked against a signed manifest
Update checks, once you turn them on

There's no telemetry and no Nugget server. Every request that leaves this device is logged on the Privacy page.

Most steps take a minute. Downloading a model to this device can take longer, depending on your connection; you'll see an estimate. You can skip any step and change everything later.

Step 4 of 6

What Double Tap needs

Double Tap drafts a reply right where you're typing. To do that, your system has to let Nugget read the text field you're in and type into it. Nothing is requested now: you'll be asked the first time you use Double Tap, and you can say no.

On this computer: Linux
AT-SPI, the Linux accessibility bus, lets Nugget read and fill text fields. Most desktops have it on. On GNOME, turn on any accessibility feature, or run this command:
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface toolkit-accessibility true
Copy
On Wayland, your desktop asks once before Nugget can use a global shortcut. On X11 no prompt is needed.
Some apps (for example, some Flatpaks and Electron apps) don't expose their text to AT-SPI; there, Double Tap falls back to the clipboard.
Other systems

Nugget only reads the window you trigger it in, only when you trigger it.
